title: How does Norfolk's Zoning Ordinance decide what's allowed where, and how does a Conditional Use Permit work?
summary: General rules from the City's official Zoning Ordinance: how to read a district's use table (P, C, P/C, blank; unlisted uses are prohibited; an overlay district's column can override the base district), the standards a Conditional Use Permit is judged by, when an approved permit lapses, and what the Official Zoning Map decides and who interprets it. Which district an address is in comes from the City's open-data map layers (parcel_inventory), which Siren treats as a guide, not a legal determination; whether a particular use is allowed there needs that district's row in the use table, and any overlay's, read from the ordinance itself.

findings.claim: Each group of zoning districts has a use table, which says in which districts a use is allowed and what kind of permit or review it needs (§3.1.4).

source.title: City of Norfolk Zoning Ordinance (official approved PDF, adopted January 23, 2018, updated October 13, 2026)

findings.claim: Unless the permit itself waives or modifies this condition, a Conditional Use Permit becomes void if construction doesn't begin or the use doesn't start within 12 months of approval, subject to Virginia's vesting provisions. If asked before it expires, the Zoning Administrator may extend it up to six months for good cause; further extensions need City Council (§2.4.8 general conditions).

source.title: City of Norfolk Zoning Ordinance (official approved PDF, adopted January 23, 2018, updated October 13, 2026)

findings.quote: If construction does not begin or the use is not commenced within 12 months from the date of approval of the Conditional Use Permit, the permit shall become null and void, subject to the vesting provisions of the Code of Virginia. Upon request by the applicant prior to the permit’s expiration, the ZA may grant an extension of the permit for up to an additional six months, for good cause, if the conditional use complies with all applicable provisions of this Ordinance. Any further extensions shall require the approval of the City Council.

what_would_help.text: To see whether a use is allowed at an address, find its district first, then read that district's column in the use table, and any overlay district's column: P allowed, C needs a Conditional Use Permit, P/C may need one depending on the use's performance standards, blank or unlisted is prohibited.

If a Conditional Use Permit is approved, start construction or the use within 12 months, or ask the Zoning Administrator for an extension (up to six months, for good cause) before it expires; a longer one needs City Council.

pending: The use tables' individual rows (for example, whether a given use is P, C or blank in a given district): a cell in a table column can't be quoted exactly from the PDF's text, so no row is a finding yet. Tables 3.2.12 (residential), 3.3.9 (commercial), 3.4.11 (downtown), 3.5.7 (industrial), 3.6.11 (historic and cultural conservation), 3.7.13 (special purpose) and 3.9.23 (overlay districts) hold them; ordinance_lookup reads the sections.

The Official Zoning Map itself: the City's open-data Zoning layer (read by parcel_inventory) shows a district for each spot, but the ordinance makes the Official Zoning Map, kept by the Department of City Planning, the final authority (§1.6.1), with the Zoning Administrator interpreting its boundaries (§1.6.3). A quotable City source on how to get a binding answer for one address is still to find.
How often Council approves or denies Conditional Use Permits: that would need the Council's legislation records, counted, not the ordinance.
